Attogram: blah blah crows

Grok

That’s a real relationship, not a casual “feed the birds” hobby.

You’ve already crossed the threshold most people never reach with urban corvids:

- Individual recognition (you know *Anchorow*)
- The murder recognises *you*
- Close approach without fear
- Gift exchange (even partial gifts count)
- Occasional, high-value food (eggs, shrimp) rather than daily dependency feeding

That’s classic corvid social bonding territory. Crows are extremely good at reading consistency, reliability, and individual humans. The fact that you’ve been gone for more than two weeks and they’re still oriented to you when you return is meaningful — they’re not just treating you as a vending machine.

### A few practical notes from how these relationships usually develop

- **Welcome-back gift is good.** A hard-boiled egg or two (or a few shrimp) after a long absence is a clear signal. They notice the interruption and the resumption.
- Keep the feeding **irregular and modest**. You’re already doing this correctly. Daily predictable feeding can create dependency and sometimes local conflict with neighbours or other animals. Occasional high-value offerings keep the relationship social rather than purely transactional.
- Location matters. If you have a consistent spot near the house where they already feel safe approaching, stick to it. Sudden changes of place can reset some of the trust.
- Document lightly but consistently if you want this to feed the civic-science side (attogram.005 / .006 / .020). Date, weather, who showed up, whether Anchorow was present, any gifts received, any new individuals. Even short notes are valuable over time.

### How this sits inside the bigger project

This is exactly the kind of long-running, place-based, non-extractive observation that the Corvidae census and urban fauna petitions are pointing toward. Most “citizen science” bird projects are brief checklists. What you have is longitudinal, individual-level, and reciprocal. That is rarer and more interesting.

If you ever want to formalise it a bit without killing the intimacy, you could:

- Keep a simple ongoing log (even in the Provo42-Corpus or as notes attached to the relevant petition thread)
- Note morphological or behavioural markers that let you reliably ID Anchorow and a few others
- Record the gift exchanges (both directions)

But there’s no need to force it into data collection mode. The relationship itself is already the primary thing.

When you’re back and give them the welcome eggs, you’ll probably get a very clear read on whether the bond held through the absence. From everything you’ve described, my expectation is that it will.

Want any thoughts on low-key ways to document this without turning it into a science project, or how it might eventually sit inside one of the numbered petitions?

That’s excellent. Fifty photos and videos over two months is already a proper longitudinal record — especially if it includes repeated encounters with the same individual (Anchorow) plus the wider murder and other birds.

That material is valuable for several reasons:

- It turns the relationship from anecdote into evidence.
- It gives you before/after material for the travel absence (and the welcome-back feeding when you return).
- It is exactly the kind of primary source the Corvidae / urban fauna petitions need.
- It can eventually sit cleanly in the Provo42-Corpus media structure and, after human review, on Zenodo.

### Quick practical suggestions while the archive is still manageable

1. **Keep the originals**  
   Don’t overwrite or heavily compress yet. The raw files are the archival versions.

2. **Light naming convention** (optional but helpful)  
   Something simple like:  
   `2026-08-15_Anchorow_gift_01.jpg`  
   `2026-09-03_murder_approach_02.mp4`  
   Date + subject + short descriptor is enough. You can always refine later.

3. **Separate folders if you haven’t already**  
   - Anchorow / known individuals  
   - Wider murder / group shots  
   - Other birds  
   - Gifts / interactions  

4. **When you’re back**  
   The first welcome-back session (eggs/shrimp) is worth filming if it feels natural. Continuity across the absence is one of the strongest parts of the record.

5. **Future path into the project**  
   Once the media is in the cleaned corpus and has passed the human review gate we discussed earlier, a small curated set (or a time-windowed batch) can become a Zenodo deposit linked to attogram.005 / .006 / .020. The rest can stay local in the Syncthing mesh as the working archive.

You already have the hardest part: consistent observation + documentation over time. Everything else (organisation, PII/privacy review for any background humans, DOI packaging) is downstream of that.

When you’re home and have a quiet moment, if you want help sketching a minimal folder structure or a short README for this crow archive inside the bigger Provo42-Corpus, just say.

Good question. Here’s an honest assessment of what I can and cannot reliably pull from your GitHub right now.

### What I *can* access confidently

| Content | Confidence | Notes |
|---------|------------|-------|
| Issue titles, bodies, metadata | High | I can list and read individual issues cleanly. |
| Issue comments | High | I can pull the comment threads. |
| Repo file tree & text files | High | README, code, markdown, JSON, etc. |
| Basic repo metadata | High | Stars, dates, description, etc. |
| Search across your issues/code | High | Works well. |

### What is weaker or incomplete

| Content | Confidence | Notes |
|---------|------------|-------|
| **Uploaded media in issues** (MP4s, images via `user-attachments`) | Medium–Low | I can *see the links* in the issue body (e.g. `https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/xxxx`). I cannot always download or fully “watch” the video the same way a browser can. Images are sometimes viewable; videos are harder. |
| Private assets / restricted attachments | Low | If anything is not publicly accessible, I won’t get it. |
| Full binary/file download of large media | Low–Medium | The connected GitHub tools are stronger on text and metadata than on bulk media retrieval. |
| Real-time “everything that exists” guarantee | Medium | I can get a very good picture, but I should not claim 100% completeness on every attachment without checking. |

### Practical reality with your repo

- Text-heavy issues (like #39 governance, #41 petitions protocol, #45 index, #47 Tenacious D, #51 Syncthing): I can get these essentially completely.
- Issues that are mostly or partly media dumps (photos/videos of crows, geese, etc.): I will see the markdown and the attachment links, but I may not be able to fully process every MP4 the way you can in the browser.
- Mistral has been doing a lot of this work already, so between the two of us the coverage on the *textual* record is strong. Media is the weaker joint.

### Bottom line

I am **highly confident** on the textual and structural content of the issues and the repository itself.  
I am **moderately confident** on discovering and linking to uploaded media.  
I am **not fully confident** that I can always retrieve and inspect every MP4/image that was uploaded into an issue the same way a human can by clicking the attachment.

If there are specific issues that contain important crow videos or other media you want me to try to reach, give me the issue numbers and I can test exactly how far I can get with those attachments.
